Complete prerequisite proofs: unbounded generators, scalar bounds and the full CAR/factor route.

Bogoliubov automorphisms and the Hilbert–Schmidt criterion

Written by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra. New original text: public domain (CC0).

A unitary change of one-particle coordinates acts on the CAR algebra. In its tracial representation this action extends normally to the hyperfinite factor. The innerness criterion below answers when its implementer belongs to that factor. Sufficiency follows from the eigenvectors of the compact difference from the identity; necessity uses a controlled diagonalizing perturbation. The eigenmode calculation constructs the local implementing matrices and their convergent product. The normal-extension and continuity theorem then describes the action as a map of topological groups. The complete analytic arguments and twelve worked problems supply the details used throughout.

The concrete CAR, its half-state trace and its completed pointed matrix product are supplied by Fermions, Fock space and quasi-free factors, Sections 10 and 15–16. The diagonal step uses the proved product-innerness theorem. Section 6 below supplies the whole analytic passage to arbitrary unitaries: the Hilbert–Schmidt ideal, compact diagonalization, interval projections, a bounded logarithm, and a dyadic diagonal perturbation with an explicit square-sum bound. It also constructs the unitary groups and the resolvent criterion needed for the possibly unbounded statement in Lemma 3.1. Its continuous calculus is the complete local ITP F03–F04, F06 and F08 argument and its scalar proofs; the underlying Hilbert estimates are ITP Sections 10.1–10.2. Normal continuity is proved directly on square-summable vector coefficients. This route uses neither a factor uniqueness theorem nor a trace-density theorem.

Throughout, KKK is a separable infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space, A=CAR⁡(K)A=\operatorname{CAR}(K)A=CAR(K), and

τ=ω1/2,R=πτ(A)′′,Hτ=L2(R,τ).\tau=\omega_{1/2},\qquad R=\pi_\tau(A)'',\qquad H_\tau=L^2(R,\tau).τ=ω1/2​,R=πτ​(A)′′,Hτ​=L2(R,τ).

6. Complete analytic support for the proof route

These supporting arguments do not add numbered results to the original six statements. They prove the exact analytic inputs used there. We work with complete complex Hilbert spaces, bounded adjoints, and the continuous calculus proved in ITP F03–F04, F06 and F08, whose scalar completeness, polynomial approximation, exponential series and Banach-valued integral proofs are in Elementary calculus for infinite products. These are local proof providers, rather than a citation to a projection-valued spectral theorem. The Hilbert-space completion, orthogonal projection, Riesz and adjoint arguments are the full ITP Sections 10.1–10.2 constructions.

6.1. The Hilbert–Schmidt space and its whole ideal estimate

A countable orthonormal basis of a separable Hilbert space is obtained by applying Gram–Schmidt to a countable dense sequence and discarding zero residuals. Each original vector belongs to the span of the residuals through its stage. The completed span is therefore the whole space. Orthogonal finite partial sums give Pythagoras; their distance to a vector tends to zero by this density. This proves Parseval. Bessel's inequality is the same finite Pythagoras estimate without totality. The assertions also cover finite-dimensional and zero subspaces.

For a bounded TTT, define

6.2. Compact self-adjoint diagonalization, including the zero eigenspace

A finite-dimensional self-adjoint operator is diagonalizable by an orthonormal basis. Here is the needed elementary proof. Its quadratic form is real and attains its maximum on the unit sphere, by finite-dimensional coordinate compactness. At a maximizing unit vector xxx, varying the normalized vector x+tzx+tzx+tz, for z⊥xz\perp xz⊥x, first with real ttt and then with purely imaginary ttt, makes both components of ⟨z,Tx⟩\langle z,Tx\rangle⟨z,Tx⟩ zero. Thus TxTxTx is a real scalar multiple of xxx. Its orthogonal complement is invariant, and induction supplies the remaining eigenvectors. In this basis the operator norm is the largest absolute eigenvalue, and the largest absolute value of its quadratic form is that same number.

For any bounded self-adjoint TTT, put m=sup⁡∥x∥=1∣⟨x,Tx⟩∣m=\sup_{\|x\|=1}|\langle x,Tx\rangle|m=sup∥x∥=1​∣⟨x,Tx⟩∣. The easy bound is m≤∥T∥m\le\|T\|m≤∥T∥. For a unit xxx, compress to the at most two-dimensional space spanned by x,Txx,Txx,Tx. The compressed self-adjoint operator sends xxx to TxTxTx, so its norm is at least ∥Tx∥\|Tx\|∥Tx∥. The finite result makes its norm a quadratic-form value, hence at most mmm. Taking the supremum over xxx gives m=∥T∥m=\|T\|m=∥T∥.

Now assume T≠0T\ne0T=0 is compact and self-adjoint; let M=∥T∥M=\|T\|M=∥T∥. Choose unit xjx_jxj​ whose quadratic-form absolute values tend to MMM, and pass to one of the two signs. With λ=M\lambda=Mλ=M or −M-M−M according to that sign,

∥(T−λ)xj∥2=∥Txj∥2−2λ⟨xj,Txj⟩+λ2≤2M(M−sgn⁡(λ)⟨xj,Txj⟩)⟶0.\|(T-\lambda)x_j\|^2 =\|Tx_j\|^2-2\lambda\langle x_j,Tx_j\rangle+\lambda^2 \le2M\bigl(M-\operatorname{sgn}(\lambda) \langle x_j,Tx_j\rangle\bigr)\longrightarrow0.∥(T−λ)xj​∥2=∥Txj​∥2−2λ⟨xj​,Txj​⟩+λ2≤2M(M−sgn(λ)⟨xj​,Txj​⟩)⟶0.

Compactness supplies a convergent subsequence of TxjTx_jTxj​; since λ≠0\lambda\ne0λ=0, the displayed estimate makes the corresponding xjx_jxj​ converge to a unit eigenvector with eigenvalue λ\lambdaλ.

Restrict to its orthogonal complement and repeat while the restriction is nonzero. Each restriction remains self-adjoint and compact. The selected eigenvectors eje_jej​ are orthonormal, and each selected ∣λj∣|\lambda_j|∣λj​∣ is the norm of the remaining restriction before that step. If infinitely many are selected, λj→0\lambda_j\to0λj​→0: otherwise the orthogonal vectors Tej=λjejTe_j=\lambda_je_jTej​=λj​ej​ would have an infinite subsequence separated by a fixed positive distance, contradicting compactness. Hence the restriction norms tend to zero. Every vector orthogonal to all the selected eje_jej​ is killed by TTT. If the procedure stops finitely, the same assertion holds by its stopping condition. A nonzero eigenspace is finite dimensional, since an infinite orthonormal sequence in it would give the same contradiction. Adding a basis of the kernel therefore gives the full orthonormal diagonalization, with every nonzero eigenvalue included.

For a compact normal TTT, its real and imaginary parts are compact self-adjoint and commute. The preceding decomposition of its real part has finite-dimensional nonzero eigenspaces invariant under the imaginary part; diagonalize on each. Its kernel is also reducing, and the compact self-adjoint diagonalization of the imaginary part on that kernel completes the basis. This proves the precise normal-compact input in Lemma 3.2.

6.7. The exact normal-functional boundary and the three different criteria

The concrete ultraweak topology is the topology of the coefficients ∑n⟨ξn,xηn⟩\sum_n\langle\xi_n,x\eta_n\rangle∑n​⟨ξn​,xηn​⟩ with both lists square summable. ITP Section 10.6 constructs the complete countable amplification and proves absolute convergence of those coefficients. A linear functional continuous for this topology is a finite linear combination of them. Indeed continuity bounds it on a neighborhood specified by finitely many such coefficients; rescaling forces it to vanish on their common kernel. It factors through the finite-dimensional image of the coordinate map to Cm\mathbb C^mCm; extending a basis of that image expresses it as a linear combination of the coordinates. Concatenating finitely many lists, absorbing the scalar coefficients into their second legs, gives one coefficient series again.

There is also a full local Banach predual identification, rather than a definition silently replacing the predual in Theorem 1.1. CAR Section 19.1 completes H‾⊗H\overline H\otimes HH⊗H in the projective norm, proves its dual is B(H)B(H)B(H) by Riesz, and represents every element by a projectively summable series. Reciprocal scalar rescaling turns that series into two square-summable lists. Quotienting by the closed subspace of coefficients vanishing on RRR yields a Banach space with dual exactly RRR: a commutator coefficient detects any operator outside R=R′′R=R''R=R′′. Hahn–Banach, proved there, identifies its quotient norm with the functional norm on RRR. Thus its image is the whole concrete R∗R_*R∗​, is norm complete, and consists exactly of the series used in (4). Theorem 1.1 proves convergence for every member of this actual predual. No L1L^1L1 identification, normal trace density, or truncation of an unbounded density is required.

The innerness assertion of Theorem 4.1 is specifically membership of an implementer in the tracial von Neumann factor RRR. Innerness on the norm-complete CAR algebra AAA requires an implementer in AAA and has the trace-class criterion for complex-linear one-particle unitaries. Fock implementability instead permits an implementer in B(F)B(\mathcal F)B(F); the selfdual formulation tests the Hilbert–Schmidt off-diagonal (1−P)VP(1-P)VP(1−P)VP relative to its Fock basis projection PPP. In the ordinary vacuum Fock representation every complex-linear uuu has its exterior second quantization: it acts by u⊗nu^{\otimes n}u⊗n on the nnn-particle antisymmetric space and by the identity on the vacuum. The completed orthogonal sum is unitary and conjugates the creation and annihilation operators correctly. It need not belong to RRR or to AAA. The CAR-algebra and general selfdual Fock equivalences are comparison statements from Araki, not additional theorems established here; the numbered statements and every exercise use only the factor criterion proved above.

A. L. Carey, Inner automorphisms of hyperfinite factors and Bogoliubov transformations, Ann. I. H. P., Physique théorique 40(2) (1984), 141–149. The definition of G2G_2G2​, Theorem 1.1/Corollary 1.2 and the parity converse give the factor comparison. For complex-linear unitaries, finite real ±1\pm1±1 eigenspaces have even dimension and the negative odd branch is excluded; the real Hilbert–Schmidt norm squared is twice the complex norm squared. Use the body, whose signs differ from the abstracts. Carey's proof invokes Araki's Fock criterion and CAR trace-class implementation, plus Ruijsenaars' vacuum phase and determinant formulas. Those are dependencies of that broader source proof, not foundations imported into the local proof above.

Huzihiro Araki, On Quasifree States of CAR and Bogoliubov Automorphisms, Publ. RIMS 6 (printed header 1970/71), 385–442; EMS article 2511, DOI 10.2977/PRIMS/1195193913, indexes 1970, no.3. Lemma 4.2, pp.389–390, and Corollary 6.2, p.401, give the state-preserving GNS comparison. Theorem 5 and its complete proof, pp.421–424, concern innerness in the CAR algebra and use trace class. Theorem 7, p.432, concerns Fock implementation and tests an off-diagonal Hilbert–Schmidt operator; its converse prints “trace class” where that hypothesis should remain Hilbert–Schmidt. The proof still invokes the earlier representation-equivalence theorem, whose full chain is not admitted here. The separate criteria are recorded in Section 6.7.

The local analytic construction uses Hilbert completion, the concrete CAR and product-innerness arguments, continuous scalar calculus and the projective coefficient predual. These exact inputs are linked in Sections 1–6. The broader source proofs of Fock implementation, vacuum determinant phases and trace-class implementation have additional prerequisites; those comparison criteria are kept separate from the tracial-factor argument.
